name: B
year_note: Created by Ken Thompson with Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs around 1969 for the PDP-7 version of Unix; Thompson's 'Users' Reference to B' for the PDP-11 is dated 7 January 1972.
tagline: Ken Thompson's typeless, word-oriented cut-down of BCPL for early Unix, and the direct parent of C.
summary: B is a small, typeless language that Ken Thompson derived from BCPL to fit the tiny PDP-7 on which Unix was born. Every value is a machine word, treated as an integer or an address depending on the operator, and its terse syntax (braces, ++, --, compound assignment) looks strikingly like early C. When byte-addressed PDP-11s made the lack of a character type painful, Dennis Ritchie extended B with types, producing C.
history:
Ken Thompson began B as an attempt at a Fortran compiler for the PDP-7, but his implementation far exceeded the available memory. Simplifying it and adapting the language to his own taste, influenced by BCPL, he arrived at a language with BCPL semantics in a new, more compact syntax; Thompson described it as 'BCPL semantics with a lot of SMALGOL syntax'. The first compiler was written in McIlroy's TMG, and B on the PDP-7 compiled to threaded code.

In 1970 B moved to the new PDP-11, where an assembler, the dc calculator, an early yacc and B itself were written in it. A separate implementation ran on Honeywell GCOS machines, described by Steve Johnson and Brian Kernighan; Kernighan's tutorial for it contains the first known 'hello, world' program. Thompson added the two-address assignment operators (=+) and invented ++ and --.

The word-only design suited the word-addressed PDP-7 and Honeywell but not the byte-addressed PDP-11, where characters had to be unpacked with library calls and floating point was awkward. From 1971 Ritchie added types, creating 'New B' and then, by 1972-73, C. B survived for years on GCOS mainframes.
innovations: The ++ and -- increment and decrement operators, in prefix and postfix forms (Thompson)
Two-address assignment operators (=+, =-, ...), taken from TMG and later reversed to C's +=
C's concise surface: braces, the ?: conditional, E1[E2] defined as *(E1+E2), and auto and extrn storage classes
A compiler small enough for the memory-starved PDP-7, used to bootstrap early Unix tools

typing.notes: One type, the machine word. On byte-addressed machines characters had to be packed and unpacked with char() and lchar(), which motivated C's types.

influenced_by.note: A stripped-down BCPL with new syntax; the word-only semantics and *n-style escapes carry over.
B began as Thompson's attempt at a Fortran compiler for the PDP-7.
The =+ operators came to B from McIlroy's TMG, which took them from ALGOL 68's +:=.

influenced_by_external.name: TMG
influenced_by_external.note: Douglas McIlroy's compiler-writing language, used to write the first B compiler.

influenced_by_external.name: SMALGOL
influenced_by_external.note: Thompson: 'BCPL semantics with a lot of SMALGOL syntax'.

structured-control.note: if/else, while and switch, alongside goto.

pointers.note: & and *, with vectors as pointers: v[i] means *(v+i).

first-class-functions.note: Function names are word values that can be stored, passed and called through; no closures.

modules.note: Separately compiled files share names through extrn declarations resolved by the linker.

milestones.event: Thompson develops B on the PDP-7 for the first Unix
B ported to the PDP-11; Unix tools written in it
Ritchie begins adding types ('New B'), leading to C
Thompson's 'Users' Reference to B'; Kernighan's B tutorial introduces 'hello, world'
Johnson and Kernighan's 'The Programming Language B' for Honeywell GCOS

trivia: Kernighan's 1972 B tutorial contains the first known 'hello, world' program, split across external variables because a GCOS B character constant held at most four characters.
Thompson never confirmed whether the name abbreviates BCPL or refers to Bon, an earlier language of his.
According to Ritchie, ++ and -- were not inspired by the PDP-11's auto-increment addressing modes, since B predates that machine.

hello.dialect: B (PDP-11 era, per Thompson's 1972 manual), via aap/b
hello.notes: printf is a library function written in B itself (Thompson's manual prints its source). *n is B's newline escape, inherited from BCPL; C changed it to \n. Declaring library functions with extrn follows Thompson's manual.

factorial.dialect: B (PDP-11 era, per Thompson's 1972 manual), via aap/b
factorial.notes: return takes a parenthesized value: return (expr);. Functions that are only called need no declaration.

fizzbuzz.notes: The loop uses while, the only looping statement in Thompson's PDP-11 manual; ++i increments before the test.

higher-order.dialect: B (PDP-11 era, per Thompson's 1972 manual), via aap/b
higher-order.notes: No lambdas: functions are words, so even and square are passed by name (declared extrn because they are used as values rather than called). auto v[10] reserves a vector on the stack, and a function body may be a single statement: even(x) return (...);

shapes.dialect: B (PDP-11 era, per Thompson's 1972 manual), via aap/b
shapes.notes: No structs or types: a shape is a 4-word vector holding a function, a string and two numbers, and s[0](s) calls through the stored function, a hand-rolled form of dynamic dispatch.

signature.title: Everything is a word (and the first hello, world)
signature.dialect: B (PDP-11 era, per Thompson's 1972 manual), via aap/b
signature.notes: The first line reproduces the external-variable example from Kernighan's 1972 B tutorial, the earliest known 'hello, world': character constants are packed into words (four per 36-bit Honeywell word, eight per word on this 64-bit implementation). Pointers and functions are words too; E1[E2] is defined as *(E1+E2), so 1[p] is legal. B's =+ became C's +=.

toolchains.name: aap/b (reconstructed B compiler)
toolchains.install: FROM debian:trixie-slim; apt-get install -y gcc libc6-dev binutils git; git clone https://github.com/aap/b /opt/b; cd /opt/b/amd64 && PATH=.:$PATH sh xx (bootstraps the self-hosted bc/ba compilers); add a bcomp wrapper that runs bc and ba, then links with cc -no-pie brt1.s <prog>.s brt2.s printn.s printf.s libb.s bilib.s
toolchains.notes: A reconstruction of Thompson and Ritchie's compiler that generates the original threaded code, with 8 characters per 64-bit word. B passes main's last expression value to exit(), so exit statuses below 128 are treated as success; only signals count as failure.

runtime.notes: BCause (github.com/Spydr06/bcause) was also tried but crashed when calling a function through a variable, a core B idiom.
